t: Program control: sequence, selection and iteration
l: Hello and welcome to Digital Tech Revision, the podcast for CCEA GCE Digital Technology. I'm Aoife.
And I'm Conor. Today's episode is lesson AP20: Program control: sequence, selection and iteration.
So Conor, if someone only remembers one thing from today, what should it be?
Explain sequence, selection and iteration with reference to a given algorithm. That is the heart of it.
Okay, take us through it properly.

Every program, however large, is built from three control structures. Sequence means carrying out instructions one after another in the order they are written, so the position of each statement matters: a total must be calculated after the values it depends on have been input and before it is output. Selection lets a program choose between different paths depending on a condition that evaluates to true or false, for example charging a different fare for a child or adding a fee only for an overweight bag. Iteration repeats a block of statements, called the body of the loop, so the same code does not have to be written out many times.
Makes sense. Keep going.

Iteration comes in two forms. Count-controlled loops repeat a number of times known before the loop starts, while condition-controlled loops repeat while, or until, a condition is met, so the number of repetitions does not need to be known in advance. These structures can be nested inside one another: a loop may contain decisions, and one loop may contain another. Being able to identify each structure in a given algorithm, choose the right one for a task, write it in C sharp and trace it by hand are all core skills tested in A S one.
Right. What else do we need to know?

An if statement evaluates a condition and runs its block only if the result is true; if it is false the block is skipped and execution continues after it. Adding else gives two mutually exclusive paths: exactly one of the two blocks will run, never both. When there are several possibilities, an else if chain tests conditions in order and runs only the first block whose condition is true, so the order of the tests matters. Arranging bands in order, lowest first or highest first, means each later condition needs only one bound, because earlier branches have already removed the other values.
Got it. Keep going.

The final else catches anything not matched, which is useful for out-of-range or unexpected data. Nested selection puts one if statement inside another, so the inner decision is only made when the outer condition has a particular result; for example, a hospital fridge monitor might first ask whether a reading is within the safe range and only then decide whether an unsafe reading is too cold or too warm. Conditions are built using relational operators and combined with and and or, as covered in AP19. Clear indentation shows which statements belong to which branch, and deep nesting should be avoided where a chain or combined condition reads more clearly.
And is there anything people often mix up here?

A switch statement compares the value of one variable or expression with a list of constant case labels and jumps to the matching case. In C sharp, each case section must end with break (or another jump such as return) so that control does not fall through into the next case; several labels can be stacked above one section so that they share the same code, for example treating 6 and 7 as weekend days. The default section runs when no case matches, acting like the final else in a chain. A switch is clearer and less repetitive than a long else if chain when a single value is being matched against fixed options, such as menu choices, day numbers or category codes, and it makes the set of options easy to see at a glance.
Okay. Keep going.

Its limitation is that the classic form tests only for equality with exact values, so it cannot directly express ranges such as age below 16; an if…else if chain is needed for those. Newer versions of C sharp do allow relational patterns in a switch, but the AS course expects the traditional form. In pseudocode, the equivalent is usually written as CASE … OF with a list of options and an OTHERWISE clause.
Go on.

A count-controlled loop is used when the number of repetitions is known before the loop begins, either because it is fixed, such as five working days, or because it has already been entered, such as the number of people in a group. In C sharp this is a for loop, whose header has three parts: initialisation of an integer loop counter, a condition checked before each pass, and an update applied after each pass, usually i++ to add one. If the condition is true, the body runs again; once it is false, the loop ends and execution continues after it. The counter can be used inside the body, for example to number prompts, and it can count down (i--) or in steps (i += 3).
Right. Keep going.

Off-by-one errors are common, so check the boundaries carefully: for (int i equals 1; i less than or equal to 5; i++) runs five times, as does for (int i equals 0; i less than 5; i++), but i less than 5 starting from 1 runs only four times. In pseudocode, a count-controlled loop is written as FOR i becomes 1 TO 5 … NEXT i, or in plain English as REPEAT 5 TIMES. The foreach loop, which visits every element of an array or list, is also count-controlled and is covered with data structures in AP22.
Go on.

A condition-controlled loop repeats while, or until, a condition is met, so it is used when the number of repetitions is not known in advance. A while loop is a pre-condition loop: the condition is tested before each pass, so if it is false at the start the body never runs at all. This suits processing a list of values that ends with a sentinel, a dummy value such as -1 that marks the end of the data and is not itself processed. The standard pattern reads the first value before the loop and reads the next value as the last statement in the body.
Makes sense. Keep going.

If the sentinel is entered first, the loop correctly processes nothing, but any later calculation such as an average must then guard against dividing by zero. A do…while loop is a post-condition loop: the body runs first and the condition is tested at the end, so it always runs at least once, which suits menus and input validation where the user must be asked at least once. The equivalent pseudocode REPEAT … UNTIL stops when its condition becomes true, which is the opposite of do…while. If nothing inside the body can change the condition, the loop never ends: an infinite loop, which is a logic error.
Go on.

Structures can be placed inside one another. With nested loops, the inner loop runs completely for every single pass of the outer loop, so the total number of times the inner body runs is the product of the two loop counts: an outer loop of 3 and an inner loop of 4 gives 12. Nested loops naturally process two-dimensional data such as seating plans, timetables, multiplication grids and the 2D arrays met in AP22. Real programs mix all three constructs, for example a validation loop to read a group size, then a for loop to process each member, with else if selection inside to place each person in a price band.
Got it. Keep going.

To check such code, use a trace table: a column for each variable and condition, and a new row each time a value changes. Work through the code one statement at a time exactly as the computer would, rather than guessing the pattern. Trace tables reveal logic errors such as off-by-one boundaries, a sentinel being added to the total, or a counter that is never updated. Meaningful names (row, col, count) and consistent indentation make nested code far easier to read, trace and debug.
Time for quickfire key terms. I'll say the term, and you give me the answer the mark scheme gives credit for.
Go for it.
Sequence?
Executing instructions one after another in the order in which they are written.
Selection?
A construct in which a condition determines which of two or more paths through the program is followed.
Iteration?
Repeating a set of instructions, either a set number of times or while/until a condition is met.
Count-controlled loop?
A loop that repeats a fixed number of times known before it starts, e dot g. a for loop.
Condition-controlled loop?
A loop that repeats while or until a condition is met, so the number of repetitions need not be known in advance.
Nested loop?
A loop placed inside the body of another loop; the inner loop completes fully for each pass of the outer loop.
What about the exam? Where has this come up?

Questions often give an algorithm and ask you to explain sequence, selection and iteration with reference to it; one mark is typically for the definition and one for identifying where it appears, so quote the relevant line, for example 'the IF total greater than or equal to 500 statement only applies the discount when the condition is true'. For the difference between count-controlled and condition-controlled loops, state that a count-controlled loop repeats a number of times known before it starts, while a condition-controlled loop repeats until or while a condition is met, and give an example of each. For while versus do…while, state where the condition is tested and the consequence: zero runs are possible with while; at least one with do…while. When asked to justify a loop choice, link it to whether the number of repetitions is known. Code-writing questions credit correct logic, sensible variable names and correct boundaries, so check less than versus less than or equal to carefully; mark schemes often accept equivalent code in any sensible form. In trace questions, write out every value in order rather than jumping to the answer. Common mistakes include processing the sentinel value, confusing UNTIL with WHILE conditions and forgetting that only the first true branch of an else if chain runs.

Let's finish with a question for the listeners. What is the key difference between a count-controlled and a condition-controlled loop? Is it A, Only condition-controlled loops use a counter; B, Count-controlled loops can never be nested; C, A count-controlled loop repeats a number of times known before it starts; D, A condition-controlled loop always runs at least once?
I'll give you a few seconds.

The answer is C: A count-controlled loop repeats a number of times known before it starts. A for loop repeats a known number of times; while and do…while repeat until a condition changes, so the number of passes need not be known.
That's it for Program control: sequence, selection and iteration. Next, try the worksheet and the quiz for this lesson on the hub.
Thanks for listening. See you next time.
